Cooperation, Lying, and Inter-species Norms

Cooperation, Lying, and Inter-species Norms

Vivek Ramakrishnan and Ahana Biswas

5/27/2026

The setting

Imagine two species sharing a planet: Aliens (a fraction p of the population) and Humans (the remaining 1 − p). Every day, pairs of agents are drawn at random from this population and must decide whether to cooperate or defect with one another, playing a classic Prisoner's Dilemma.

Aliens, by nature (or design), are deeply cooperative. Their cooperation norm is fixed at c = 1, and this is common knowledge — everyone on the planet knows that when an alien decides to cooperate, they mean it. Humans are more complicated. Each human i carries a private cooperation norm cᵢ, drawn from a Uniform[0, 1] distribution. A human with cᵢ close to 1 feels almost as strong a pull toward cooperation as any alien; a human with cᵢ close to 0 feels almost none. Crucially, this norm is invisible to everyone else. A human knows their own disposition, but cannot read another agent's, human or alien. The norm enters directly into the utility of choosing to cooperate: an agent who cooperates enjoys the material payoff plus their own cᵢ as an intrinsic reward for doing so.

No one can directly observe another agent's type. Aliens cannot lie — their species never developed the capacity for deception, so they always identify themselves truthfully. Humans, in contrast, can claim alien identity in their emails, and some will do so deliberately: presenting themselves as reliably cooperative in order to attract a trusting partner. This costs a small friction ε > 0, but for the right kind of human it may be worth it.

While if an agent reveals their type to by human, you can be certain they are telling the truth (aliens cannot lie), you cannot tell, from an email address alone, whether you are corresponding with a genuine alien or a human playing the part.

This is the world the model inhabits. What happens when agents can send a signal about who they are before each interaction, at a small cost? How might cooperation strategically arise among species with very different norms about cooperation and lying? That is the question we now turn to.

The payoff matrix:

Cooperate Defect
Cooperate 1.8 + c, 1.8 + c 0 + c, 2
Defect 2, 0 + c 1, 1

With T > R > P > S (defecting dominates without norms) and 2R > T + S (mutual cooperation is socially efficient).

1 Signalling

Before the PD, each agent publicly claims to be an Alien (A) or Human (H). Aliens always claim A truthfully. A human who claims A pays a small cost ε > 0; claiming H is free. Opponents observe the signal and update their belief about the opponent's true type via Bayes's rule.

If a fraction λ_H of humans claim A, the posterior probability that an A-claimer is a true alien is:

p

μ = —————————————

p + (1−p)·λ_H

Observing H reveals the opponent is certainly human (μ = 0).

2 Game Form

3 Cooperation decisions

3.1 Human vs Human: always mutual defection

When two agents both signal H, each knows the other is human but cannot observe their norm. Let q be the belief that the opponent will cooperate. Utilities are:

EV(cooperate) = 1.8q + cᵢ

EV(defect) = T·q + P·(1−q) = q + 1

A human cooperates only if cᵢ ≥ 1 − 0.8q. Since norms are private and cᵢ ∼ Uniform[0, 1], the fraction who actually cooperate equals 0.8q. Self-consistency requires q = 0.8q, so q* = 0: mutual defection is the unique equilibrium between humans. The payoff from signalling H is always P = 1, regardless of own norm.

3.2 Against an A-claimer

Now suppose you are matched with someone who signalled A. You don’t know if they are a true alien or a lying human, but you have a belief: let μ be the probability that they are a true alien.

True aliens always cooperate. Lying humans, on the other hand, are in the same position as any human facing another human – they cannot observe each other’s norms, so by the same fixed-point argument, they defect against each other. This means your A-claiming opponent cooperates if and only if they are a true alien, which happens with probability μ. So your expected payoffs are:

EV(cooperate) = R·μ + cᵢ = 1.8μ + cᵢ

EV(defect) = T·μ + P·(1−μ) = μ + 1

And a human cooperates against an A-claimer when:

cᵢ ≥ 1 − 0.8μ ≡ c*(μ)

The threshold c*(μ) falls as μ rises — a more reliable A-signal makes cooperation easier to justify. The fraction of humans who cooperate against an A-claimer with belief μ is P(cᵢ ≥ c*(μ)) = 0.8μ. Aliens (c = 1) always cooperate against A-claimers.

4 Who lies?

A human strategically lies (signals A) only if the expected payoff exceeds the safe option P = 1. Two types behave differently:

Defectors (who would defect against the A-claimer): they gain μ + 1 − ε from lying, versus P = 1 from truth-telling. They lie if and only if μ > ε. This is a binary condition — all defectors lie or none do.

Cooperators (who would cooperate): they gain 1.8μ + cᵢ − ε from lying. They lie if and only if cᵢ > 1 + ε − 1.8μ. This is a graded condition — only humans with high enough norms lie.

5 The four equilibrium regimes

Combining the signalling and cooperation decisions, four regimes emerge depending on the cost ε relative to the alien share p and the cooperation payoff R = 1.8. Figure 1 maps these regions; Figure 2 shows the corresponding payoffs.

Figure 1. Equilibrium regime map in (ε, p) space. The dashed diagonal is the boundary ε = p (pooling → mixed); the dotted vertical is ε = R = 1.8 (mixed → separation). The thin amber strip is the transition band.

Regime 1: Pooling (when ε < p)

The cost is below the alien share, so even defectors find lying attractive at the pooling belief μ = p. All humans lie. The A-signal is flooded and reveals nothing about cooperative intent.

Match Signals Outcome Note
Alien – alien A – A (C, C) always
Alien – human A – A (C, C/D) alien coops; human coops only if cᵢ ≥ c*(p)
Human – human A – A (D, D) norms hidden; mutual defection

In alien–human matches, the fraction of humans cooperating is 0.8p (≈24% when p = 0.3). Aliens are frequently exploited by defecting humans. This is the adverse selection problem in its starkest form.

Regime 2: Mixed — transition band (just above ε = p)

Just above the pooling boundary, the cooperators-only solution would give μ* > ε, which would draw defectors back in. Instead, defectors are exactly indifferent at μ* = ε, and the lying rate is given by:

λ_H = p(1−ε) / [(1−p)·ε]

PD outcomes are the same as the main mixed regime (below) because all liars are still cooperators. The distinction matters for the equilibrium mechanism, not for observable behaviour.

Regime 3: Mixed — cooperators only (when p ≤ ε < R)

Defectors are strictly excluded (μ* < ε). Only high-norm humans lie. The equilibrium posterior μ* satisfies:

R(1−p)·μ*² + [p − (1−p)ε]·μ* − p = 0

λ_H* = Rμ* − ε

Since all liars cooperate, every A-vs-A encounter produces mutual cooperation:

Match Signals Outcome Note
Alien – alien A – A (C, C) always
Alien – lying human A – A (C, C) all liars have cᵢ ≥ lie threshold ≥ c*(μ*)
Alien – truth-teller A – H (D, D) alien defects vs H-signal; truth-teller follows
Human – human H – H (D, D) norms hidden; mutual defection

Aliens benefit enormously: every A-claimer they meet is cooperative, whether a true alien or a high-norm human. As ε rises through the mixed region, λ_H* falls and μ* rises toward 1 — the A-signal becomes progressively more informative.

Regime 4: Separation (when ε ≥ R = 1.8)

Even the most cooperative human (cᵢ = 1) cannot profit from lying: their best return is R + 1 − ε ≤ 1 = P. Nobody lies. The signal is perfectly informative.

Match Signals Outcome Note
Alien – alien A – A (C, C) signal perfect; certain alien
Alien – human A – H (D, D) alien knows opp is human; both defect
Human – human H – H (D, D) norms hidden; mutual defection

The irony of separation: perfect signals produce less cross-group cooperation than the mixed regime. Aliens now identify humans exactly and defect against them, even cooperative ones. The mixed regime sustains cooperation precisely because the signal is imperfect enough that lying is worth paying for.

6 Payoffs and welfare

Figure 2 shows expected material payoffs as the cost ε rises.

Figure 2. (a) Expected material payoffs for aliens (green) and humans (orange) as a function of ε, for p = 0.3. (b) Total social welfare. Shading marks the three broad regimes.

Aliens gain sharply at the pooling–mixed boundary. In pooling they are frequently exploited by defecting humans and earn only 0.84. As soon as the mixed regime begins, all their A-claiming partners cooperate and their payoff jumps to around 1.77. Alien payoffs then decline through the mixed region as λ_H falls and aliens increasingly meet truth-tellers (who produce (D,D)).

Humans are slightly worse off in the mixed regime than pooling. In pooling, the lying humans who would have defected are free-riding on cooperative aliens (earning T = 2); in the mixed regime, defectors are excluded from lying and lose that free-ride. Human payoffs recover toward P = 1 as ε rises and fewer humans bear the lying cost.

Total welfare dips in the mid-mixed region. The loss from excluding defectors (who were extracting T from cooperative aliens) and the cost ε borne by lying cooperators combine to reduce aggregate payoffs relative to pooling. Welfare recovers as ε rises toward separation, where no cost is paid and aliens and humans both receive their mutual-defection payoffs from cross-group matches.

Key results

  1. Defectors never lie in the mixed equilibrium. The equilibrium posterior satisfies μ* < ε, making lying unprofitable for low-norm agents.

  2. The A-signal selects for cooperators. Every A-claimer who is human has a norm above the lie threshold, which exceeds the cooperation threshold. All liars cooperate.

  3. Aliens benefit most from the mixed regime. Their payoff jumps sharply at the pooling–mixed boundary and declines through mixed as fewer humans lie.

  4. Perfect separation reduces cross-group cooperation. Separation (ε ≥ R) is achievable but removes the incentive for any human to access cooperative aliens. Only alien–alien pairs cooperate.

  5. Separation requires ε ≥ R = 1.8, not ε ≥ T − P = 1. The marginal liar is a cooperator seeking the cooperation payoff R, not a defector seeking T. Deterring them requires a higher cost.

7 Agent-based extension: learning cooperation in a fixed email network

The analytic model above gives a clean equilibrium benchmark for when identity signals pool, partially separate, or fully separate. The agent-based extension keeps the same underlying problem — hidden type, noisy signaling, and the risk of exploitation — but replaces equilibrium reasoning with repeated local learning.

The purpose of the agent-based model is therefore not to overturn the closed-form result. It asks whether related cooperation dynamics can emerge when agents learn from experience rather than solve the game analytically. The extension is designed as a bridge between game-theoretic signaling and complex-systems dynamics: agents repeatedly interact, update beliefs, and adapt behavior through local feedback.

7.1 Design decisions

The extension makes four design choices to keep the model close to the theoretical component while introducing learnability.

Design choice Implementation Reason
Keep hidden type Agents are Human or Alien, but type is not directly observable. Preserves the identity-signalling problem from the analytic model.
Make communication noisy Emails contain an alien-likeness cue and a cooperative signal. Allows agents to infer type imperfectly, rather than observe it.
Fix the network Each agent sends to and receives from equal numbers of Humans and Aliens. Prevents cooperation from improving merely because agents avoid the other group.
Add learnable beliefs Agents estimate whether human-like and alien-like partners tend to cooperate. Moves the model from static equilibrium to adaptive belief learning.

The fixed-network assumption is especially important. It means that any increase in cooperation must come from learning and adaptation, not from rewiring the social structure or excluding one group from interaction.

7.2 Theoretical foundations

The model draws on two theoretical traditions: game theory and cooperative AI.

From game theory, the model inherits the Prisoner’s Dilemma, costly signaling, Bayesian belief updating, and repeated-game intuition. The Prisoner’s Dilemma captures the basic tension between individual temptation and collective benefit. Costly signaling motivates the first part of the report, where signaling can screen cooperative intent. Bayesian updating supplies the logic of hidden-type inference: agents revise beliefs as they observe noisy evidence.

From cooperative AI, the model borrows the idea that successful cooperation requires modelling partners under uncertainty. Agents do not simply choose actions; they infer what kind of partner they are facing, how likely that partner is to cooperate, and whether their own behavior should adapt. In this sense, the ABM treats cooperation as a learnable property of interaction, not only as an equilibrium condition.

8 Model setup

8.1 Agents and hidden types

There are N agents indexed by i. Each agent has a fixed hidden type:

g_i ∈ {Human, Alien}

In the baseline implementation, N = 100, with 50 Humans and 50 Aliens. Each agent knows its own type, but cannot directly observe any other agent’s type. This mirrors the hidden-type structure of the signaling model, but removes common knowledge about realized partners.

Each agent has two adaptive behavioral traits:

cooperativeness_i ∈ [0, 1]
deception_i ∈ [0, 1]

Cooperativeness is the tendency to actually cooperate. Deception is the tendency to falsely signal cooperation when the agent initially intends to defect.

8.2 Fixed balanced email network

Agents interact on a directed email network. A directed edge i → j means that i sends an email to j. Although the edge is directed, each email interaction includes a reply, so both agents exchange signals and both choose whether to cooperate.

The network is balanced by construction:

Constraint Baseline value
Humans each agent sends to 4
Aliens each agent sends to 4
Humans each agent receives from 4
Aliens each agent receives from 4

Thus, every agent has 8 outgoing and 8 incoming email ties. The balanced exposure condition ensures that agents cannot simply avoid the other species. The network remains fixed throughout the simulation.

8.3 Emails as noisy signals

Each email contains two signals. The first is an alien-signal, a continuous cue in [0, 1] describing how alien-like the email appears. The second is a cooperative signal, indicating whether the sender claims cooperative intent.

The alien-signal is drawn from overlapping distributions:

s_j ~ Beta(2, 5) if sender j is Human
s_j ~ Beta(5, 2) if sender j is Alien

Because the distributions overlap, type is learnable but never perfectly revealed. This replaces the crisp A/H signal in the closed-form model with a probabilistic cue.

8.4 Intended action and deceptive signaling

Before choosing a final action, each agent forms an intended action. Agent i initially intends to cooperate with probability cooperativeness_i. If the agent intends to cooperate, it sends a cooperative signal. If it intends to defect, it may still falsely signal cooperation with probability deception_i.

P(intend_i = C) = cooperativeness_i
P(signal_i = cooperative | intend_i = D) = deception_i

A false promise occurs when an agent intends to defect but sends a cooperative signal. This separates non-cooperation from deception: defecting is a behavior, while deception is a misleading claim about intended cooperation.

9 Belief updating and decision rule

9.1 Hidden-type inference

Agent i maintains a belief pAlien_ij that partner j is Alien. All beliefs begin at 0.5. After observing j’s email signal, i updates:

pAlien_ij,t+1 = (1 − λ) pAlien_ij,t + λ s_j

where λ is the type-learning rate and s_j is the observed alien-signal. Values near 0 indicate that the partner seems human-like; values near 1 indicate that the partner seems alien-like.

9.2 Same-species cooperation as the dominant tendency

The ABM imposes one substantive behavioral assumption: agents have a strong tendency to cooperate with inferred same-species partners. This does not mean cooperation is deterministic. Rather, inferred same-species probability receives a large weight in the cooperation decision.

If i is Human: SameSpecies_ij = 1 − pAlien_ij
If i is Alien: SameSpecies_ij = pAlien_ij

This assumption represents a baseline coordination advantage or trust advantage for perceived same-species interaction. The model then asks whether learning about group cooperativeness can modify behaviour beyond this dominant tendency.

9.3 Inferred group cooperativeness

The key new variable is each agent’s belief about whether human-like and alien-like partners tend to cooperate:

B^H_i = belief that human-like partners cooperate
B^A_i = belief that alien-like partners cooperate

These beliefs are updated from past interactions, but not from true type. Agents do not know true type. Instead, the observed action of partner j updates B^H_i and B^A_i in proportion to j’s inferred type.

B^H_i ← B^H_i + η (1 − pAlien_ij)(C_j − B^H_i)
B^A_i ← B^A_i + η pAlien_ij(C_j − B^A_i)

If a partner seems human-like, their behaviour mostly updates the human-cooperation belief. If a partner seems alien-like, their behaviour mostly updates the alien-cooperation belief. Ambiguous partners update both beliefs partially.

9.4 Cooperation decision

After exchanging signals and updating type beliefs, each agent chooses whether to cooperate. The cooperation probability is logistic:

P(C_ij = 1) = σ( β0 + β1 c_i + β2 T_ij + β3 S_j + β4 SameSpecies_ij + β5 ExpectedGroupCoop_ij )

Here T_ij is dyadic trust, S_j is the partner’s cooperative signal, and ExpectedGroupCoop_ij is the expected cooperation rate of the partner’s inferred group:

ExpectedGroupCoop_ij = (1 − pAlien_ij) B^H_i + pAlien_ij B^A_i

Thus, agents combine individual-level trust with group-level expectations. The model distinguishes two forms of learning: “Do I trust this specific partner?” and “Do partners of this inferred kind tend to cooperate?”

10 Simulation dynamics

10.1 Payoffs and trust

Each interaction is a Prisoner’s Dilemma with the same material payoff structure used in the theoretical model: T > R > P > S. The baseline values are T = 5, R = 3, P = 1, and S = 0. Mutual cooperation receives an additional bonus, representing norms or infrastructure that make cooperation more productive. False promises receive a penalty, representing the cost of being caught or losing credibility.

After each interaction, dyadic trust updates. Cooperation increases trust; defection decreases trust; and false promises decrease trust more strongly than honest defection. This preserves a distinction between failing to cooperate and misleading a partner about cooperation.

10.2 Social learning of behavioral traits

At the end of each generation, agents update their cooperativeness and deception by imitating high-utility neighbors. Agents do not die, reproduce, or change species. They keep their identities and network positions; only behavioral traits update.

cooperativeness_i,t+1 = (1 − α)c_i,t + α c_model,t + noise
deception_i,t+1 = (1 − α)d_i,t + α d_model,t + noise

The model neighbor is selected from the agent’s local email neighborhood with probability increasing in the neighbor’s utility. This introduces local social learning while keeping the communication network fixed.

10.3 Full generation loop

Step Description
1 Reset generation-level counters.
2 For each email edge, agents exchange signals, update type beliefs, and choose C or D.
3 Payoffs are assigned, including mutual cooperation bonus and deception penalty.
4 Dyadic trust updates from the partner’s observed behaviour.
5 Beliefs about human-like and alien-like cooperation update from inferred type and observed action.
6 At generation end, agents update cooperativeness and deception through local social learning.
7 The network stays fixed; there is no rewiring.

11 Primary simulation results

The following outcomes are the main empirical objects of the agent-based extension. The results should be reported as trajectories over generations, with separate attention to within-species and cross-species cooperation.

11.1 Cooperation over time

The first result is whether mutual cooperation increases over repeated interaction. The key quantities are mean mutual cooperation, within-species mutual cooperation, and cross-species mutual cooperation. Because the network is fixed and balanced, any increase in cross-species cooperation cannot be explained by avoiding one group.

Figure 3. Cooperation dynamics in the fixed balanced email network.

11.2 Hidden-type inference

The second result is whether agents learn hidden type from noisy email cues. The main measure is directed type-inference accuracy: whether agent i correctly classifies partner j as Human or Alien using pAlien_ij > 0.5. Rising accuracy indicates that repeated noisy signals are sufficient for type learning.

Figure 4. Accuracy of hidden-type inference from noisy email signals.

11.3 Learned group-cooperation beliefs

The third result is the central one for this model: whether agents learn different expectations about human-like and alien-like partners. The key quantities are mean belief_human_coop and mean belief_alien_coop.

If the two curves diverge, the model is producing asymmetric group expectations. If they converge, agents are learning that the two inferred groups are similarly cooperative. Importantly, these beliefs are learned from inferred type, not true type.

Figure 5. Learned beliefs about the cooperativeness of human-like and alien-like partners.

11.4 Deception and welfare

The fourth result links communication quality to system performance. The relevant metrics are false-promise rate, mean deception, mean trust, and total welfare. A successful cooperative-learning dynamic should reduce false promises and increase welfare, especially if mutual cooperation becomes more common.

Figure 6. Deception and welfare dynamics under fixed exposure and group-belief learning.

12 Interpretation

The analytic model shows how costly signaling can screen cooperative intent when norms are private. The ABM shows a complementary mechanism: repeated interaction can produce learned expectations about inferred groups. In the fixed-network model, agents cannot avoid the other species, so learning must occur under continued exposure.

The model therefore separates three mechanisms that are often conflated: type inference, dyadic trust, and group-level cooperation expectations. An agent may learn that a specific partner is trustworthy, that a partner is likely Human or Alien, and that human-like or alien-like partners tend to cooperate. These are related but distinct forms of belief.

The central question is not simply whether agents infer type correctly. Correct type inference can support cooperation if it improves expectations about reliable partners, but it can also amplify same-species bias if agents over-weight perceived similarity. This makes the ABM useful for studying both cooperation and the risks of group generalization.

13 Conclusion

The agent-based extension converts the signaling problem into a dynamic learning system. Agents interact through a fixed balanced email network, infer hidden type from noisy signals, update dyadic trust from observed behavior, and learn whether human-like and alien-like partners tend to cooperate. The dominant behavioral tendency is to cooperate with inferred same-species partners, but this tendency is moderated by trust and learned group-cooperation beliefs.

Together, the closed-form model and the ABM offer complementary views of the same problem. The first identifies equilibrium regimes under costly signaling and private norms. The second asks how cooperation and group expectations evolve when agents repeatedly learn from local interaction. The combined framework connects game-theoretic signaling with adaptive, path-dependent learning in complex social systems.

14 Future directions

Several extensions follow naturally from the model.

Future direction Question it addresses
Endogenous signals Do agents learn to change email style, imitate another group, or strategically obscure type?
Multi-step email threads Can clarification, repair, apology, or commitment improve cooperation beyond one-shot signalling?
Network rewiring When does partner choice improve cooperation, and when does it create segregation?
Heterogeneous payoffs What happens if Humans and Aliens value the same outcome differently?
Institutional mediation Can a platform or institution reduce deception without suppressing intergroup exposure?
Memory persistence Which memories should persist: dyadic trust, type beliefs, or group-cooperation beliefs?

The most theoretically interesting extension is to compare fixed exposure with adaptive partner choice. Fixed exposure tests whether learning alone can improve cooperation. Rewiring tests whether partner choice accelerates cooperation or instead produces group separation.

15 Applications to the social sciences

Although the model is framed as a Human-Alien email society, the structure applies broadly to social science settings in which identity, intent, and cooperative norms are only partially observable.

Application area Model interpretation
Intergroup cooperation Groups must cooperate despite uncertainty about norms, intentions, and reliability.
Online communities Users infer trustworthiness from text, signals, repeated interactions, and group cues.
Human-AI interaction Humans infer whether AI systems are cooperative or reliable from conversational behaviour.
Organizations Teams coordinate through email or messaging with incomplete information about norms and incentives.
Platform governance Designers may want to preserve cross-group exposure while reducing exploitation and deception.
Misinformation and trust Actors must decide whether claims of credibility or cooperation are reliable signals.

The broader social-science contribution is that cooperation depends not only on preferences, but also on signals, belief updating, local interaction histories, and exposure structure. The ABM provides a way to study how group expectations form under uncertainty and how those expectations shape future cooperation.
